artworks.title: Eos
artworks.description: De Morgan's Pre-Raphaelite dawn goddess steps from the sea in rose and gold, scattering dew from a water-jar as the night peels away behind her. The canvas isolates Eos as the daily renewer — light made flesh, not yet the lover who will steal Cephalus or mourn Memnon. Oil on canvas.

artworks.title: Aurora Taking Leave of Tithonus
artworks.description: Solimena catches the dawn's cruel gift: Aurora rises from the bed of Tithonus, already immortal and already wasting, as she leaves to open the day. The Getty canvas is the Homeric hymn condensed — the goddess who asked Zeus for endless life and forgot to ask for youth. Oil on canvas, J. Paul Getty Museum.

artworks.title: Aurora and Cephalus
artworks.description: Carracci's Farnese Gallery fresco shows Aurora carrying the sleeping hunter Cephalus skyward — the dawn goddess who steals mortal beauty for her chariot. Painted for the Carracci cycle in the Palazzo Farnese, it fixes Eos as abductor and lover in one airborne embrace. Fresco, Farnese Gallery, Rome.

artworks.title: Eos and Memnon (Louvre G 115)
artworks.description: On this Attic red-figure kylix signed by Douris, Eos lifts the body of her son Memnon after Achilles has killed him at Troy — the dawn goddess as mourner, wings spread over the Ethiopian king. One of the Louvre's most famous images of maternal grief in archaic vase-painting. Musée du Louvre, Paris.

artworks.title: Aurora and Tithonus
artworks.description: Ricci's oil returns to the dawn bed: Aurora, already radiant, turns from the ageing Tithonus she cannot keep young. The Royal Collection canvas gives the myth its Venetian lightness — love, immortality, and the morning that will not wait. Oil on canvas, Royal Collection.

popCulture.title: Tithonus
popCulture.creator: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
popCulture.description: Tennyson's dramatic monologue is Eos' gift gone wrong: immortality without youth, the dawn goddess's lover wasting forever as she renews each morning.
